title: Construction is the only major industry where productivity fell for half a century
dek: American construction is the only major industry with long-term productivity decline—not from insufficient capital, not from wages rising too fast, not from excess profits, but from accumulated friction stacking up across the whole industry.
why: Want to know whether the reason housing gets more expensive—‘why buildings cost more to build’—is regulation, industry structure, or labor issues? This episode systematically rules out popular explanations and builds a clear logical chain worth following all the way through.
who: Anyone working on or investing in real estate development costs, construction tech, or urban housing policy; and general readers interested in why housing keeps getting more expensive.
skip: The first two minutes of setup about the background of a 1968 report can be skipped without affecting understanding of the core argument that follows.

points.h: Construction is the only major industry where productivity fell for half a century
points.body: Syverson and Goolsbee found U.S. construction productivity grew from the 1950s through the late 1960s, even faster than the overall economy. But it's been falling for 50 years since. This is unprecedented—Syverson stresses no other industry shows this pattern. Technology normally drives productivity gains that multiply. The fact that construction once did grow means it wasn't always immune; something specific broke at a turning point.

points.h: Rising capital per worker proves it's not money—the problem is structural
points.body: Syverson checked all the popular theories one by one. Capital per construction worker kept pace with the broader economy—so not under-capitalization. Wages and material costs didn't rise faster than in other industries. Profit margins didn't spike abnormally. The only real anomaly: construction prices rose faster than overall inflation, yet worker output per person—adjusted for house size and quality—has been flat since the mid-1970s. No actual efficiency gains.

points.h: The incentive structure rewards chasing the next job over finishing this one well
points.body: Syverson points out construction's incentive structure is fundamentally broken. Once a company lands a contract, its attention shifts immediately to the next bid rather than perfecting the current job. The industry's money comes from landing new deals, not from smooth execution—poor work still gets paid. This creates no industry-wide drive to improve processes. The profit motive points the wrong way.

points.h: Zoning killed the chance to build at scale by fracturing land into tiny pieces
points.body: Glaeser sees regulation as the key variable. Minimum lot sizes range from one or two acres up to 60 acres in parts of San Francisco. Wetland definitions are drawn so broad—one town defined it as ‘a giant muddy area’—that they block almost any project. Together these rules make large-scale production impossible. Glaeser admits the evidence isn't airtight, but this is his preferred hypothesis.

points.h: Construction's 600,000 tiny firms lock it out of the scale economies
points.body: The U.S. construction industry has nearly 600,000 firms with fewer than 5 employees, but only 101 establishments with over 1,000 workers. Manufacturing, by contrast, has 171,000 small firms and 990 large ones—a completely different shape. Land is increasingly fragmented into small parcels. This ‘small sites, small firms’pattern locks the industry structurally out of scale economies. California's push for backyard accessory units is worth trying, but it's not mass production.

points.h: Katerra spent over $800 million and couldn't rewrite 150 years in two years
points.body: Katerra, founded by Tesla's former interim CEO with more than $800 million from SoftBank, attempted to overturn every aspect of construction at once and went bankrupt in 2021. Buckley says they failed by trying to rewrite 150 years of industry history in just two years—money can't solve a structural time problem. Rupnik disagrees: Katerra's real legacy was positive. It proved that modular methods running successfully overseas for 30–40 years actually work technically. Some factories and staff were acquired by other companies and continue operating.

points.h: Singapore mandated 70% offsite construction on public projects to force industry capacity
points.body: Hough notes that Singapore mandates at least 70% offsite construction on government projects, and this regulatory demand catalyzed a strong prefab industry. But he highlights the chicken-and-egg problem: the U.S. is only at around 6% modular construction. Mandating 70% instantly would fail because factories can't scale production without upfront policy signals. Companies need government commitment before they'll invest in building the capacity.

points.h: Pay double or triple for existing homes, buy them out, abolish density restrictions
points.body: Glaeser proposes a thought experiment for high-cost metros like Silicon Valley, Boston, and New York: pick certain zones where government or developers buy out existing owners at two to three times current prices at a generous rate, then eliminate all density restrictions. Allow ‘by right’construction up to 50 stories as long as it meets safety codes. This would draw developers exploring how to build cheaply and at scale, shifting supply toward average buyers instead of wealthy ones.

quotes.text: My view is, to have a sector this big, to have so many problems for so long, it just seems odd that it would be one thing that if you just turned that off, everything would magically get better.
the most important thing, rather than being good at what you’re already doing, is to just get started even in an inefficient way at the next thing

incumbent owners have figured out how to use a maze of rules and regulations to protect what they have, and to make sure that they don’t have any sort of inconvenience. But people do pay a cost for it. And the cost is paid by outsiders.
one town in the survey that we did 15 years ago actually defined wetlands as a “wicked big puddle.”
They’re trying to revise 150 years of history in two by throwing a few billion dollars at it. It didn’t work.

We are in a spiral. And that spiral requires us not to just encourage more people to enter the industry, create more education, or generally invest in new building materials. It requires a complete shift in the way that we are building today in order for us to maintain our output tomorrow.
